title: The Gleaner's Handful
hook: a gleaner's family gives away its last barley, and a school of atoms opens with the same word: dharma
carry: even a school of atoms begins with dharma
tomorrow: a father tells his son to break a seed. what's inside?

segments.voice: Yesterday Nyaya ended with Nachiketa, who held his doubt at Death's door until he was taught. A second school opens today.

After the great war, King Yudhishthira holds a horse sacrifice so lavish that everyone says nothing like it has ever been seen. Then, in the middle of all the praise, a mongoose crawls out of a hole. Half its body is gold. And it speaks: this whole sacrifice, it says, isn't worth a little barley flour that a poor gleaner once gave away in Kurukshetra.
screen: `A KING'S GREAT SACRIFICE.` → `A HALF-GOLDEN MONGOOSE.` → `NOT WORTH A HANDFUL OF BARLEY.`

segments.voice: This is from the Mahabharata. The gleaner lived by unchha: picking up the grains left in the fields after harvest, one by one. In a famine, he, his wife, his son and his son's wife scraped together a little barley. Just as they sat to eat, a hungry guest arrived. The gleaner gave him his share. The guest was still hungry. His wife gave hers, then the son, then the son's wife. Then the guest revealed who he was: Dharma himself. The mongoose had rolled in the flour left on the floor, and half of it turned gold. Ever since, it has gone from sacrifice to sacrifice, looking for one great enough to gild the other half. Now today's school, Vaisheshika, credited to a sage named Kanada. Tradition says his name comes from living like that gleaner, on grains, kana, gathered one by one. Whether or not that's history, his book fits it. You'd expect a school of atoms to open with matter. The Vaisheshika Sutra opens with dharma: now we will explain dharma, that from which come rising in this world and the highest good. Before it counts a single particle, it says why counting matters. And tradition links its name to vishesha, particularity: what makes each thing this one and not another. So the teaching, plainly: for this Hindu school, knowing what the world is made of serves dharma. Put the gleaner beside it, and here's our reading: dharma is done in particulars. This grain, this guest, this handful. The gleaner's gift wasn't big. It was given. Today, the particular thing in front of you counts.
screen: `THE GLEANER GIVES HIS LAST BARLEY.` · `THE GUEST IS DHARMA.` · `KANADA: KANA, A GRAIN.` · `THE SUTRA OPENS WITH DHARMA.` · then, large: `DHARMA IS DONE IN PARTICULARS.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal, take one grain of rice, or one crumb, and really look at it: someone grew it, someone carried it, it's this one. Many Hindus offer food before eating, and some say a verse from the Gita, brahmarpanam: the offering is Brahman. If you pray, offer the meal that way, or in your own words. If you don't, say a quiet thank-you for this particular plate.
Vaisheshika. The school of Kanada, linked by tradition to vishesha, particularity, and known for its atoms. Its sutra opens with dharma.
Your line: even a school of atoms begins with dharma. A gleaner's handful outweighed a king's sacrifice. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Vaisheshika is studied with Nyaya, often as one joined system, through the Vaisheshika Sutra and its commentaries; in many Hindu homes food is offered before it's eaten and treated as too sacred to waste.

chat.meaning: In the Mahabharata, a gleaner family's last barley, given to a guest who was Dharma, outweighed a king's grand sacrifice. Vaisheshika, credited to Kanada the grain-gatherer, opens with dharma and with each thing's particularity.

tie.story: A starving gleaner family gave their last barley to a guest who turned out to be Dharma, and a mongoose said it outweighed a king's sacrifice.
tie.friend: Priya can see Nani's twenty minutes as dharma in particulars: every grain is food, and none is just another one.
tie.you: what small thing could you treat as if it mattered today?

Kanada.meaning: the sage credited with the Vaisheshika Sutra

unchha.meaning: gleaning: living on grains left after harvest

vishesha.meaning: particularity: what makes this one, not that one

dharma.meaning: right conduct; here, what brings rising and the highest good

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva (the half-golden mongoose; the gleaner of Kurukshetra and his family give their barley to a guest who is Dharma)
Vaisheshika Sutra 1.1.1–2 (now, therefore, dharma; dharma defined)
Prashastapada, Padarthadharmasangraha (vishesha as what distinguishes eternal substances such as atoms)
